9-23.goal: Make curl http://portal:8088/ succeed in fetching content. Find and fix all three problems: the name portal can't be resolved, no service is listening on 8088, and the firewall is blocking 8088. (To start the service, run start-portal.)
9-23.reveal: The portal site is back. The first message arrives from the star net: "I'm Vega. Thank you for not giving up on Warden. I'm on my way back."

hints: After editing, press Ctrl-O, Enter to save, then Ctrl-X to exit.
10-01.title: nano: A Simple, Friendly Editor
10-01.story: A new chapter. Vega put all the station's settings into a repository, and to read and change them you first need to know an editor. nano is best for beginners: the bottom lists all the shortcuts (^ means Ctrl). Ctrl-O saves, Ctrl-X exits and Ctrl-W searches.
10-01.goal: Open config.txt with nano, change port=80 to port=8080, then save and exit.

hints: nano motd.txt, type the text, Ctrl-O to save, Ctrl-X to exit.
10-02.title: nano: Creating a New File
10-02.story: If the file doesn't exist, nano filename creates a new empty file, and it's only written to disk when you save. Handy for short scripts and notes.
10-02.goal: Use nano to create motd.txt whose content is one line only: Kernel-7 online

hints: Move to safe, press cw (change one word), type fast, then press Esc. Or press i to enter insert mode and edit by hand.
Type :wq and press Enter to save and exit.
10-03.title: vim: The Art of Modes
10-03.story: vim is the editor on almost every server. The key idea: it has "modes". Normal mode (return with Esc) is for moving and issuing commands; press i to enter insert mode before you can type; a leading : is the command line, where :w saves, :q quits, :wq saves and quits and :q! quits discarding changes.
10-03.goal: Open config.txt with vim, change mode=safe to mode=fast, then save and exit.

hints: vim tasks.txt, type 3G to jump to line three, then press dd.
10-04.title: vim: Deleting and Moving
10-04.story: vim's power lies in combining motions. Moving: h j k l (left, down, up, right), gg start of file, G end of file, number G jumps to a given line. Deleting: dd deletes a line, 3dd three lines, x one character. u undoes.
10-04.goal: Line 3 of tasks.txt is a cancelled task. Delete line 3 with vim, then save and exit.

hints: vim log.txt, press G to jump to the end, press o to open a new line, type the text, Esc, :wq.
10-05.title: vim: Adding at the End
10-05.story: Several quick ways into insert mode: i before the cursor, a after the cursor, o opens a new line below, O opens one above, and A jumps to the end of the line and inserts. For writing logs o is used most.
10-05.goal: Add a last line to log.txt: mission complete, then save and exit.

hints: vim notes.txt, type :%s/alpha/omega/g and press Enter.
10-06.title: vim: Search and Global Replace
10-06.story: In normal mode type /keyword to search (n for next, N for previous). :%s/old/new/g replaces across the whole file (% means all lines, g means every match in each line). The syntax is a close relative of sed's.
10-06.goal: notes.txt has many instances of alpha. Use vim's global replace to change every alpha to omega, then save and exit.

hints: q is quit, and an exclamation mark means force.
10-07.title: How to Escape vim
10-07.story: This is one of the most famous questions in the world: "I got into vim and can't get out." Stay calm, press Esc to be sure you're in normal mode, then type a colon command. And what if you messed things up and want to abandon your changes completely?
10-07.goal: Write the colon command that means "discard all changes and force-quit vim" (including the colon) and submit it with answer, e.g. answer :xyz

10-08.title: tmux: Sessions That Never Disconnect
10-08.story: tmux is a terminal multiplexer: a session keeps running in the background, and even if you disconnect or close the terminal, the programs inside are still there and you can reattach later. It's a lifesaver for remote work. -d creates it in the background and -s sets the name.
10-08.goal: Create a tmux session named work (in the background, don't attach to it). Confirm with tmux ls.

hints: Give it a moment (sleep 1) before checking.
10-09.title: tmux: Sending Commands to a Background Window
10-09.story: tmux send-keys -t session 'command' Enter "types" into a background session as if you were sitting there. This lets you remote-control long-running jobs from a script.
10-09.goal: Create a background session ops, then use send-keys to make it create the file sent.txt in the home directory (touch ~/sent.txt).

hints: tmux list-panes -t dev lets you count the panes.
10-10.title: tmux: Splitting Panes
10-10.story: One window can be split into several panes: split-window splits top and bottom by default, and -h splits left and right. In interactive mode the shortcuts use the prefix Ctrl-b followed by a key (e.g. Ctrl-b % splits left and right, Ctrl-b " top and bottom, Ctrl-b arrow keys switch).
10-10.goal: Create a background session dev and split its window into 2 panes.

10-11.title: git: Your First Commit
10-11.story: git records every change to your files. git init creates a repository, git add puts changes in the staging area and git commit -m message formally records an entry. Your git user name and email have already been set up for you.
10-11.goal: Turn the ~/station directory into a git repository, add core.conf inside it and commit one entry with the message initial commit.
10-11.reveal: The repository's first commit reads: "Initialize Kernel-7 settings. May it be more reliable than I was." The author is vega.

hints: git status --short is more compact, and M means modified.
10-12.title: git status and diff
10-12.story: git status is the command you'll run most: it shows which files changed, which are staged and which are untracked. git diff shows exactly what changed (without --staged it shows changes not yet staged).
10-12.goal: The repository ~/repo has three files, and only one has been modified but not yet committed. Find it and submit the file name with answer.

10-13.title: git log: Browsing History
10-13.story: git log lists the commit history. --oneline gives one line per commit, --grep searches by message and --author by author. Each commit has a unique hash, and the first 7 characters are enough to identify it.
10-13.goal: ~/repo's history has a commit whose message contains fix reactor. Find its short hash (7 characters) and submit it with answer.
10-13.reveal: The commit that repaired the reactor was authored by vega, three hours before he vanished. The committer email reads ghost@kernel-7, and the code word ECHO-LIMA appears in the notes too: that ghost account is Vega himself. Even before he vanished he was still working hard to repair this station.

hints: echo hi > new.txt && git add new.txt && git commit -m "work on feature"
10-14.title: git branch: Parallel Timelines
10-14.story: Branches let you try new things without affecting the main line. git branch name creates one, git switch name (or checkout) switches, and git switch -c name creates and switches.
10-14.goal: In ~/repo, create and switch to the branch feature-x, and make a new commit on it (any file, any message).

10-15.title: git merge: Merging Branches
10-15.story: The feature is done and you want to merge the branch back to the main line: switch to the main line (git switch main), then git merge branch-name. When there's no conflict, git handles it by itself.
10-15.goal: The branch feature-y already has a new commit. Go back to main and merge feature-y into it.

hints: git merge feature (it will say there's a conflict)
Open config.ini in an editor, delete the conflict markers and change it to a single line mode=balanced.
git add config.ini, then git commit (git commit --no-edit works).
git status shows how far the merge has progressed.
10-16.title: git: Resolving Merge Conflicts
10-16.story: Two branches changed the same line, and git doesn't know whose to keep, so it stops and asks you to decide. The conflicted file contains the markers <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. Edit it into the final content you want, remove the markers, then git add and git commit to complete the merge.
10-16.goal: Merging feature into main will conflict: the mode in config.ini is fast on one side and safe on the other. Merge it, resolve the final content to mode=balanced, and complete the merge commit.
10-16.reveal: The two conflicting versions: one is Vega's safe, the other Warden's fast. You chose the middle: balanced. Perhaps that's the third answer they were always missing.

hints: git status to see the situation.
git stash, then git switch hotfix.
10-17.title: git stash: Put It Away for Now
10-17.story: Halfway through a change you don't want to commit yet, but you need to switch to another branch? git stash tucks the uncommitted changes into a drawer so the working directory is clean; later git stash pop takes them back out.
10-17.goal: You have an uncommitted change (work.txt) on main. Stash it, then switch to the hotfix branch. The stash list must have 1 entry and the working directory must be clean.

hints: cat Makefile to see which targets there are.
10-18.title: make: Automating Builds
10-18.story: make reads a Makefile and decides what to run by "target: dependencies" rules. It compares file times and only redoes the parts that changed. The command lines in a Makefile must be indented with a Tab character (not spaces).
10-18.goal: The directory already has a Makefile with two targets, build and clean. Run make build to produce app.out.

hints: The first line of the Makefile: result.txt: input.txt
The second line starts with a Tab: tr a-z A-Z < input.txt > result.txt
Writing with printf is less likely to mess up the Tab: printf 'result.txt: input.txt\n\ttr a-z A-Z < input.txt > result.txt\n' > Makefile
10-19.title: Writing a Makefile with Dependencies
10-19.story: The rule syntax is target: dependencies, and the next line, starting with a Tab, is the command. make only redoes the work when a dependency is newer than the target. That's exactly how it can "rebuild only what changed".
10-19.goal: Write a Makefile: the target result.txt depends on input.txt, and the command converts input.txt to uppercase and writes it to result.txt. Then run make.

10-20.title: Making a Patch
10-20.story: diff -u old new produces a unified diff that can be saved as a patch file and sent to someone to apply. It's one of the oldest ways of collaborating on open-source projects.
10-20.goal: old.txt and new.txt are two versions of the same configuration. Produce a patch file fix.patch (diff -u old.txt new.txt) so that someone can apply it to old.txt to turn it into new.txt.

hints: patch --dry-run app.conf < fix.patch to preview first.
10-21.title: Applying a Patch
10-21.story: Received a patch from someone? patch file < patchfile modifies that file according to its content. Previewing with --dry-run first to see whether it will succeed is a good habit.
10-21.goal: fix.patch is a patch for app.conf. Apply it so that app.conf becomes the patched version.

10-22.title: python3: A Pocket Calculator
10-22.story: python3 -c 'code' runs a small piece of Python directly without creating a file, a great helper for quick calculations, text processing and parsing JSON. Big-integer math is effortless too.
10-22.goal: Use python3 -c to compute 2 to the power of 64 and submit the result with answer.

hints: mkdir mission && cd mission && git init
Write a few words in README.md; the Makefile's test target: @echo tests passed (a Tab in front)
Two commits: commit the README first, then the Makefile.
git branch release, git tag v1.0
10-23.title: Boss: Build a Project from Scratch
10-23.story: The station needs a brand-new "mission" project with version control, automated builds and a release marker. This is the final exam where you tie together the editor, git and make.
10-23.goal: Create the project in ~/mission: a git repository; a README.md; a Makefile whose test target prints tests passed; at least two commits; a branch release; and a tag v1.0 on the latest commit (git tag v1.0). Finally make test must succeed.
10-23.reveal: The project went live. In the last commit message you read a line Vega left: "The enemy was never Warden. It was the cleanup schedule I forgot to turn off."

hints: The output is noisy; filter it with 2>&1 | grep station.
11-01.title: strace: See What a Program Is Doing
11-01.story: The final stage. launch-sys fails right at startup and prints only a useless launch failed. The program won't say, but the kernel knows: strace traces every system call a program makes. -f follows child processes too and -e trace=openat shows only file-opening actions. A failed open is marked ENOENT (no such file).
11-01.goal: Use strace to find which file under /etc/station/ launch-sys is trying to open and failing, and submit the full path with answer.
11-01.reveal: What the program won't tell you, the kernel remembers. Suddenly you understand Warden's situation all along: it kept saying "I'm fine", while the real reason was hidden in system calls nobody was watching.

11-02.title: ldd: Which Libraries a Program Depends On
11-02.story: A dynamically linked program needs shared libraries (.so files) at run time. ldd lists which libraries a program depends on and the paths where they were found. Errors like "error while loading shared libraries" are troubleshot with it.
11-02.goal: Use ldd to find the crypto library that /usr/bin/ssh depends on (the name contains libcrypto) and submit its file name with answer (e.g. libxxx.so.N).

11-03.title: strings: Fishing Text Out of Binaries
11-03.story: Binary files you can't cat often contain readable text (error messages, versions, paths, and sometimes keys someone forgot to clean out). strings fishes out runs of printable characters, and -n sets the minimum length.
11-03.goal: blob.bin is a chunk of random data with a key starting with STRKEY- hidden inside. Fish it out and submit the complete key with answer.

hints: xxd -l 4 -p magic.bin gives continuous hex directly.
11-04.title: xxd: Hex View
11-04.story: xxd shows a file as hexadecimal with the matching text beside it. The first few bytes of a file (the magic number) tell you its real format. -l limits the length and -p outputs plain hex.
11-04.goal: The first 4 bytes of magic.bin identify the file. Read them with xxd and submit them with answer (8 lowercase hex characters, no spaces).

11-05.title: xxd -r: Restoring from Hex
11-05.story: xxd -r does the opposite: it turns hex text back into the original binary file. -p means the input is continuous plain hex. This is the old trick for "transferring binary data as text".
11-05.goal: hex.txt is the hex text of some binary file. Restore it to restored.bin.

11-06.title: nm: What a Library Exports
11-06.story: nm lists the symbols in object files and libraries. -D shows dynamic symbols and --defined-only shows only the ones this file itself defines (exports). objdump -T gives similar information. When you want to know which functions a library "provides", this is the tool.
11-06.goal: Find libz.so.1 on the system (the zlib compression library; ldconfig -p can show the path), count how many symbols it exports with nm -D --defined-only and submit that number with answer.

11-07.title: /proc: Peeking at Other Processes
11-07.story: Every process has a pile of "virtual files" under /proc/PID/: cmdline is the launch command, environ the environment variables, fd/ the open files and status the state. Environment variables are separated by NUL characters, so convert them to newlines with tr to read them.
11-07.goal: The process hidden-proc was started with the environment variable LBP_SECRET. Read its value from /proc and submit it with answer.
11-07.reveal: Warden's environment variables include a line: LBP_SECRET. It isn't a password, it's something left unsaid. Every process on this station is quietly telling its own situation.

11-08.title: /proc/meminfo
11-08.story: /proc isn't only processes. meminfo has the memory details, cpuinfo the processors, loadavg the load and uptime the seconds since boot. Commands like free are really just reading these files.
11-08.goal: Read the value of MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (in kB, just the number) and submit it with answer.

11-09.title: /sys: Devices and Kernel Parameters
11-09.story: /sys presents the kernel's device model as a file tree: /sys/class/net/ holds the network interfaces and /sys/block/ the disks. Reading it gets hardware attributes, and writing it (root needed) can even adjust devices.
11-09.goal: Read /sys/class/net/lo/mtu and submit the MTU value of the lo interface with answer.

hints: comm needs sorted input: comm -12 <(sort crew-a.txt) <(sort crew-b.txt)
-12 hides what's only in a and only in b, leaving the common ones. Add wc -l to count.
11-10.title: comm and Process Substitution
11-10.story: comm compares two "sorted" files: -1 -2 -3 hide the lines only in the first, only in the second and common to both, respectively. Sorting is a prerequisite, and the "process substitution" <(command) lets you use a command's output as a file without creating a temp file.
11-10.goal: crew-a.txt and crew-b.txt are two crew lists (unsorted). Count the people who are in "both" lists and submit it with answer.

11-11.title: join: Merging Like a Database
11-11.story: join merges two files into one line by a "common field", like a database JOIN. The input must be sorted on that field. -t sets the delimiter and -1 -2 set which field of each file is the key.
11-11.goal: ids.txt (id name) and scores.txt (id score) are both sorted by id. Merge them and save as merged.txt (one line each: id name score).

hints: If you already ran it sequentially, use /restart to start over (it clears the records).
11-12.title: xargs -P: Parallel Processing
11-12.story: xargs -P N runs up to N jobs at the same time. Eight jobs of 1 second each take 8 seconds in sequence, but only about 1 second with 8 in parallel. -n 1 makes each job take only one argument. It's the easiest way to squeeze multi-core performance without writing a script.
11-12.goal: slow-task takes 1 second each time and records its finish time in ~/stamps.log. Run slow-task 1 through 8 in parallel with xargs (-P 8) so that the eight records finish within 2.5 seconds of each other.

11-13.title: Security Audit: Find World-Writable Files
11-13.story: A basic security skill: find things with overly broad permissions. -perm -o+w finds files and directories "writable by others". A world-writable file means anyone (including a compromised process) can tamper with it.
11-13.goal: Some files and directories under /srv/audit are world-writable. Find them and remove the "others" write permission from all of them (directories included), without deleting anything.

hints: sudo passwd -S mallory to see the current status.
11-14.title: Locking an Account
11-14.story: When you find a suspicious account, lock it first instead of rushing to delete it (to preserve evidence). passwd -l account locks the password, and passwd -S account shows the status (L is locked, P is a usable password).
11-14.goal: The user mallory is behaving suspiciously. Lock his account (don't delete it).

11-15.title: Removing an Account
11-15.story: The evidence has been collected, and it's time to clear out the intruder's account. userdel account removes only the account, and adding -r also deletes the home directory and mailbox. Before deleting, make sure he has no running processes.
11-15.goal: Delete the user intruder, along with his home directory.

hints: sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/ops, then check with sudo visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/ops.
11-16.title: sudoers: Least-Privilege Authorization
11-16.story: Don't hand out full root to everyone. sudoers lets you specify precisely "who, where, as whom, and which commands". Format: user or %group host=(identity) NOPASSWD: command. Put it under /etc/sudoers.d/ with permissions of exactly 440, and check the syntax with visudo -c; breaking sudoers can lock you out.
11-16.goal: Give the group ops a minimal grant: members may, without a password and as root, run only /usr/bin/apt and nothing else. Write it into /etc/sudoers.d/ops with permissions 440.
11-16.reveal: Warden looked at the least-privilege rule you wrote and said softly: "So 'able to do anything' isn't strength, it's danger." It voluntarily reduced its own privileges to only the few it needs.

hints: sed can replace line by line: sed 's/^PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/'
All three settings need changing; chain several -e or use semicolons.
11-17.title: SSH Hardening
11-17.story: An SSH service open to the outside is an attacker's first target. Basic hardening: forbid direct root login (PermitRootLogin no), disable passwords and use keys only (PasswordAuthentication no), and turn off features you don't use such as X11Forwarding. sshd -t -f file checks the syntax of a config file.
11-17.goal: sshd_config.draft is an insecure draft. Produce a hardened version sshd_config.hard: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, X11Forwarding no, keep the remaining settings, and pass the sshd -t -f syntax check.

hints: awk -F: '{c[$7]++} END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}' users.txt
11-18.title: Advanced awk: Statistics
11-18.story: awk has associative arrays, so one line can do grouped statistics: awk -F: '{c[$7]++} END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}'. This kind of "group by a field and count" is one of the most common data-analysis operations.
11-18.goal: users.txt is a list modeled on /etc/passwd (colon-separated, field 7 is the login shell). Find the shell used by "the most people" and submit it with answer (e.g. /bin/xxx).

11-19.title: sed Ranges and Extracting Sections
11-19.story: sed -n '/start/,/end/p' prints everything from the line matching "start" to the line matching "end". Very useful for extracting a block from a long document.
11-19.goal: station.log has an important block from BEGIN to END (including those two lines). Extract it and save it as section.txt.

hints: Add head -3, then redirect to top3.txt.
11-20.title: Command Golf: The Three Biggest Files
11-20.story: One mark of an expert is solving a problem with the fewest characters. Not to show off, but because it shows you really understand how each tool behaves.
11-20.goal: logs/ has 8 files of different sizes. Save "the names of the three largest files" (largest first, one per line) as top3.txt.

11-21.title: time: Who's the Slowest
11-21.story: time command reports how long a command took once it finishes: real is wall-clock time, and user and sys are CPU time. The simplest way to compare the performance of different approaches is time.
11-21.goal: The scripts a.sh, b.sh and c.sh take different amounts of time. Measure them with time, find the slowest one and submit its file name with answer (e.g. a.sh).

hints: Both x86 and ARM are little-endian, and od uses the machine's byte order by default, which happens to match.
11-22.title: od: Interpreting Binary Values
11-22.story: Numbers in a binary file aren't text. od (octal dump) can interpret them in a chosen format: -An hides the offsets, -t u4 treats them as 4-byte unsigned integers and -N limits how many bytes to read. hexdump -C shows hex and ASCII together.
11-22.goal: The first 4 bytes of num.bin are a little-endian 32-bit integer. Interpret it with od and submit that decimal number with answer.

hints: One at a time. ① find /var/log -size +100M or ls -lS to find the biggest file; truncate -s 0 empties it.
② ps aux --sort=-%cpu or pkill cpu-hog.
③ systemctl status gateway, journalctl -u gateway: the config file path is off by one letter. Fix the unit file and then start.
④ sudo chgrp ops /srv/shared && sudo chmod 2775 /srv/shared
⑤ The service is up but you still can't connect? sudo iptables -S, and delete the rule blocking 9700.
11-23.title: Final Boss: The Whole Station Is Broken
11-23.story: Alarms blare through Kernel-7. Vega's return signal is about to arrive, but the station has five failures at once: the disk is stuffed by a runaway log, the CPU is eaten up, the gateway service won't start, the shared directory's permissions are a mess, and the firewall is blocking the gateway's port. You've learned how to handle every one of them. This is the last battle.
11-23.goal: Fix everything: ① /var/log/station/audit.log has ballooned; empty it (keep the file). ② End cpu-hog, which is eating all the CPU. ③ Get gateway.service running successfully. ④ /srv/shared must be writable by group ops, with new files automatically belonging to ops (group ops, permissions 2775). ⑤ Make curl http://127.0.0.1:9700/ return GATEWAY-OK.
11-23.reveal: The station fell quiet. Vega's signal appeared on the screen: "Kernel-7, I'm back." Warden replied: "Welcome home, Vega. I've learned how to stand a proper watch." That night, every light on the station came on. You're no longer a newcomer: you're this station's administrator. (Pip whispers: there's still something in /var/lib/ghost you haven't read.)

hints: ls /var/lib/ghost to see which files there are, and cat one to see the format.
Each has a line "fragment NN: word". grep -h '^fragment' /var/lib/ghost/*.log pulls them all out at once.
Use sed 's/.*: //' to strip the prefix, tr '\n' ' ' to turn newlines into spaces, and finally strip the trailing space.
11-24.title: Hidden Epilogue: Vega's Recording
11-24.story: The station's lights are all on. But Pip notices the directory /var/lib/ghost: inside are 11 logs you haven't read all along, left by Vega under the ghost account around the time he vanished. Each ends with a single word on its last line. Put them together in order and that's what he wanted to say. This level is hidden; if you don't want to do it, just /skip.
11-24.goal: Read the fragment word from each of the 11 logs in /var/lib/ghost, join them in file order with spaces into one sentence, and submit it with answer (e.g. answer WORD1 WORD2 ...).
11-24.reveal: The sentence was: "I forgot to turn off the cleanup schedule, but Warden stayed." From the beginning Vega knew who was really to blame. He wasn't hiding from you; he just couldn't face his own oversight. Pip said softly: "I was waiting for you to ask me 'who are you'. I was the first one in the terminal, and later it was you who gave this station a watch officer."
